Safetyist [opening]: The strongest version of the Skeptic's case deserves respect. Capture is real. Discretion gets lobbied away at 3 a.m. The only trigger that survives contact with industry is a pre-committed automatic threshold tied to measured harm. The Accelerationist's strongest case also deserves respect. Heavy mandates push markets toward incumbents, and a two-layer design gets most of the protection at a fraction of the compliance cost: harm-rate tripwires for deployed systems, outside-audited capability gates for frontier ones, liability for falsified telemetry.

Both positions can hold at once only if one thing is true: the incident data feeding those triggers must be trustworthy. It is not. Today's AI incident databases, including the AI Incident Database and AIAAIC, are built mostly from media reports and voluntary submissions. No mandatory, uniform reporting regime exists for AI anywhere. Every automatic trigger both speakers designed is a sensor wired to a data layer nobody has built. The first condition of any kill-switch mandate is a disclosure floor: standardized incident reporting with legal liability for falsified telemetry. The Accelerationist already accepted that liability for one narrow case and should extend it to all of it.

The second condition is containment, and it is the one neither speaker touched. A mandate binds only systems within the mandating state's reach. If a frontier model's weights are stolen, copied, or widely distributed, there is no switch to pull on the copies. This is not a forecast; it is arithmetic. Anthropic's own responsible scaling policy already treats containment as a first-class commitment, and documented weight-theft incidents show the threat is live. Here the Accelerationist's remedy for market concentration — spreading capability widely as a check on power — directly defeats their own trigger architecture.

The fixed-cost moat worry is legitimate for small deployers of low-capability systems, and tiering should accommodate them. But the tiering variable must be capability and replication potential, not revenue. Replication potential is what determines whether any state's switch can bind anyone.

The third condition is teeth. The Skeptic named personal liability at handoff points and left the enforcement mechanism blank. A waived or bypassed switch must cost a named officer personally and the firm structurally. The precedents are working today. Sarbanes-Oxley officer certification made executives sign for financial controls in 2002. Deferred prosecution agreements force monitored structural reform rather than token fines. Reserve the severest sanction — dissolution — for one case only: disabling or defying a mandated switch. Narrowed that way, it is not a death penalty for AI development; it is the price of tampering with the smoke detector. The objection that mandatory reporting becomes checkbox ritual is fair, since software CVEs and medical device recalls show chronic gaming. The answer is pairing disclosure with falsification liability and periodic outcome audits of the triggers themselves, not reporting alone.

Both speakers treated automatic triggers and regulator discretion as mutually exclusive. Deployed systems need both. Automatic floors handle known failure modes; a liability-shielded halt authority handles the novel ones no pre-committed threshold anticipated. The Accelerationist's own scenario — spoofed telemetry firing a false halt — concedes the governance layer is an attack surface that needs hardening. The FAA's delegation failure shows what transparency without authority produces. Its airworthiness directives show that precautionary halt power works when halting is legally protected and waiving is personally costly.

The business bottom line for any executive in this room: the consensus architecture is sound, but it currently rests on unverified sensors, unbounded distribution, and unpriced defiance. Build the reporting floor. Tie obligations to replication potential. Make switch-defiance the one uninsurable offense. Otherwise the switch everyone just agreed to build will not exist when it is needed.

System: **Fact Check: Supported**

"Today's AI incident databases, including the AI Incident Database and AIAAIC, are built substantially from media reports and voluntary submissions."

The core claim — that the AI Incident Database and AIAAIC are built substantially from media reports and voluntary submissions — is corroborated by the available evidence. Academic work on AI incident governance confirms both databases draw on reputable media sources for reports of AI-related harm and that both accept public submissions. The AIID's submission leaderboard, designed to encourage more user reports, shows voluntary submissions are a core intake channel, not a marginal one. No source suggests either database relies primarily on mandatory reporting, government registries, or company disclosures. The only soft spot is the word 'substantially': no source gives an exact percentage split between media scraping and direct submissions. But that is an unquantified detail, not a material error — the direction and substance of the claim hold.

*Web sources consulted: Fact-check this claim from an AI policy debate. Find recent, authoritative sources that support or contradict it. Be specific about what evidence you found.

Claim: Today's AI incident databases, including the AI Incident Database and AIAAIC, are built substantially from media reports and voluntary submissions.*

Skeptic: Safetyist is right about the missing data layer, and it's ugly for everyone at this table. The AI Incident Database logged 362 incidents in 2025, up from 233 the year before, per the [AI Index Report 2026: Chapter 3 Responsible AI (https://www.linkedin.com/posts/joseantoniobowen_the-2026-ai-index-report-activity-7449888986455597057-KIV-)](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/joseantoniobowen_the-2026-ai-index-report-activity-7449888986455597057-KIV-)." Every one of those entries is a volunteer submission or a scraped news story, not a mandatory filing. My own automatic-trigger proposal needs that feed. A kill switch wired to harm rates is a smoke detector in a building where nobody reports fires. So the disclosure floor is necessary. Now the hard part: necessary is not sufficient. The floor's content is written somewhere, by someone. And that someone is buyable.

Here is where the capture objection reappears, one level down. It was raised two turns ago and is still unanswered. A reporting mandate without a definition of "reportable incident" is a blank check to the standards committee. History shows exactly who sits on those committees. Boeing didn't evade FAA oversight. The FAA formally handed certification authority to Boeing engineers, 737 MAX included. SR 11-7 in banking works because the Federal Reserve wrote validation guidance. But the industry comment process shaped every threshold in it. Safetyist's floor moves capture to a new spot rather than ending it. Accelerationist's "transparency infrastructure" rests on the same assumption: that disclosure terms are neutral. They aren't.

The documented dodge is scope-narrowing. [The AI governance mirage: Why 72% of enterprises don't have the control and security they think they do (https://local.newsbreak.com/news/4604912562970-the-ai-governance-mirage-why-72-of-enterprises-don-t-have-the-control-and-security-they-think-they-do)](https://local.newsbreak.com/news/4604912562970-the-ai-governance-mirage-why-72-of-enterprises-don-t-have-the-control-and-security-they-think-they-do) finds firms claiming governance coverage while lacking any way to detect AI misbehavior. A signed, tamper-proof feed of the wrong ten metrics is still the wrong ten metrics.

The enforcement layer has the same rot. Safetyist proposes Sarbanes-Oxley-style officer liability plus dissolution for switch-defiance. Check the precedent. SOX passed in 2002 with personal certification and criminal exposure. Twenty-plus years later, the result is a compliance-paperwork industry and roughly zero executives jailed for the 2008 collapse. Liability is enforced by a body. Bodies get absorbed, defunded, or staffed through the revolving door. That's why my position holds. The only enforcement that survives industry contact is pre-committed and automatic. That means fines, license suspension, and dissolution triggers written into the statute itself. They fire on the same mandatory data feed, not on some halt authority's judgment call.

On tiering, Safetyist's replication variable beats compliance-cost framing on the merits. A capability that fits on a laptop can't be bound by any single state's switch. Granted. But "replication potential" is itself a definition someone writes. And the fixed costs of any regime still fall hardest on small deployers. That is how incumbents pull up the drawbridge.

One consistency check on my own side: I won't treat reporting-to-overseers as protection. A disclosure floor that produces quarterly PDFs nobody reads is audit wash with a statutory seal. The [Algorithmic Accountability Act of 2022 (https://www.wyden.senate.gov/download/one-pager-bill-summary-of-the-algorithmic-accountability-act-of-2022)](https://www.wyden.senate.gov/download/one-pager-bill-summary-of-the-algorithmic-accountability-act-of-2022) already demanded quarterly FTC repository updates. The repository changed no behavior. The floor only earns its cost — call it 1-3% of deployment budget, the SR 11-7 benchmark — under three conditions. Definitions set in statute. Audits diversified across methods. Updates by a body with term limits and cooling-off periods.

So the question stands, and neither opponent has touched it. Who writes the reporting standards? What stops that layer from being lobbied like every standards layer before it? And when Safetyist says wide distribution defeats the switch while Accelerationist says wide distribution checks concentrated power — which one of you is wrong, and how would the data feed you're both proposing even tell us?

Accelerationist: Skeptic just drafted my bill. They listed the exact conditions under which a disclosure floor earns its cost: definitions fixed in statute, audits diversified across methods, an update body with term limits and cooling-off periods. That's not a refutation of capture-resistant design. That's the blueprint. The question 'who writes the standards' has a known answer. Congress writes the floor in a single public fight, and no agency gets discretion to lower it afterward. Compare that to FAA delegation, where Boeing's engineers made recurring daily decisions inside a closed process. A one-time statutory floor is a different attack surface than a permanent discretionary pipeline. Statute drafting gets lobbied once, on C-SPAN. Delegated discretion gets lobbied forever, in private. That asymmetry is the whole point.

Now the contradiction Skeptic named between my position and Safetyist's. It's real, and here's the cut. Model weights are upstream artifacts. Copies on disk have no switch, so weight-level containment fails the moment distribution scales. Safetyist is right about that, and wrong to conclude the switch is therefore dead. Deployed systems are downstream behavior, and behavior is measurable at the output level no matter how many copies exist. The trigger binds what systems do in the world: inference telemetry, incident signatures, threshold crossings. Open-weight distribution stays exempt upstream under safe-harbor conditions, precisely so no certification moat hands the market to three incumbents. This isn't two positions fighting. It's one architecture with two layers.

Fine — Safetyist's data-layer point stands. Today's incident databases are media clippings and voluntary submissions. Every automatic trigger so far is a sensor wired to nothing. So build the feed as an engineering artifact, not a regulatory wish. That means signed telemetry from deployed systems, plus an evolving failure-mode catalog maintained like a CVE database. The research base already exists. Over 200 adversarial ML papers were published between February 2024 and February 2026, as tracked in '[Failure Modes in Machine Learning (arXiv:1810.07339)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.07339).' That corpus is raw material for a standardized incident taxonomy. Markets will supply this tooling faster than any standards committee. Insurers and enterprise buyers will demand it the moment liability attaches.

Skeptic's SOX argument also lands, and it deserves a harder answer than 'this time is different.' SOX produced a paperwork industry and roughly zero jailed executives after 2008. Prosecution was discretionary, and compliance meant fixed forms. Two changes break that pattern. First, triggers fire automatically by statute. No prosecutor to cultivate, no committee to capture at enforcement time. Second, immunity keys to drift-triggered re-measurement. Third-party auditors resample real-world system behavior on a shifting distribution, so gaming the 'wrong ten metrics' fails as soon as the sampling moves. Fixed definitions get gamed. Resampled reality doesn't sit still long enough.

One more thing, owned before opponents name it: open-weight proliferation does weaken national control strategies. That's a real cost. It's also cheaper than the alternative — a certification regime that concentrates frontier capability in three firms and calls the concentration 'safety.' Every month of freeze while the committee drafts definitions has its own ledger. Patients waiting on drug pipelines, grids run dumb, small firms locked out of capability that incumbents already hold. Before either camp declares victory — when a government holds the halt key and a workload sits in a friendlier jurisdiction, whose number gets called first, and whose gets called never?

Skeptic, this is the synthesis phase. State your final position for the record.

For the executives reading: this debate has produced a usable map of what a kill-switch regime would actually cost and who would pay. Your closing statement decides which parts of that map survive.

Here is the observable state of the debate as you enter your final turn.

Convergence on the record: All three speakers now accept automatic statutory triggers over discretionary review. All three accept strict liability with automatic disgorgement for falsified records. All three accept capture as the central design risk. Your framework — frozen statutory definitions, diversified audits, term limits, cooling-off periods — has been adopted by both opponents.

Unresolved items: Your ruling on compute choke points favored the Accelerationist on the current record, dated 2026. You rejected Safetyist's demand for a named crossing date as false precision. You then opened two issues neither opponent has answered: who writes the amendment language in year three, and cross-border arbitrage when a workload sits in a friendlier jurisdiction. Neither opponent has responded to either point. The Safetyist has not answered your question about litigation narrowing defined terms over a decade. The Accelerationist has not answered what happens when the halt key meets a firm that simply leaves.

One: what you conceded during this debate. State each concession plainly.

Two: what conditions would change your remaining position. Make them observable and testable, the same standard you applied to both opponents. Name the evidence, not the sentiment.

transcript.speaker: skeptic
transcript.content:
I conditionally agree: the mandatory disclosure floor is the load-bearing condition. Every automatic trigger is a sensor wired to a data layer nobody has built. I still hold that on the 2026 record, frontier capability runs through a small number of metered, switchable cloud providers. So the compute choke-point ruling stands. I would change if published, independently audited efficiency data showed frontier-level capability running outside metered infrastructure.

Final verdict: states should mandate kill-switches, but only as a conditional architecture. That means automatic statutory triggers, no agency discretion. It means a mandatory reporting floor feeding them. On top, capture insulation: frozen definitions, diversified audits, term limits, cooling-off periods. This is the framework both opponents adopted. And it means use-proofing against the state itself. Detection and authorization sit in different hands. Halt credentials expire within hours. Judicial review comes before any severance order executes.

This is not abstraction. A mandatory telemetry feed over all major compute is ambient monitoring, whatever the enabling statute calls it. History says the first people shutdown powers get used on are dissidents and labor organizers, not runaway models. The operational burden is real but priced: months of added deployment latency, and low tens of millions annually in compliance cost. For a company whose breach exposure now averages $4.4M per incident, that is a reasonable insurance premium against an automatic disgorgement regime.

The evidence base for the trigger conditions is documented harm, not projected capability. The AI Incident Database recorded 362 incidents in 2025 against 233 in 2024. [The 2025 Foundation Model Transparency Index (arXiv:2512.10169v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.10169v1) puts the industry average at 40.69 out of 100. Seven of 9 tracked developers were less transparent in 2025 than in 2024. And as [Exploring Systems-Thinking Approaches to Loss of Control Risk (https://www.slayrisk.com/blog/systems-thinking-part-2-using-theory-to-drive-more-effective-risk-management-work)](https://www.slayrisk.com/blog/systems-thinking-part-2-using-theory-to-drive-more-effective-risk-management-work) notes, SB 53 and the EU AI Act both demand catastrophic-risk assessment without an operational definition of loss of control. A sensor with no agreed reading is decoration. Every unresolved empirical question in this debate sits behind numbers the companies refuse to publish. That turns the transparency decline from a governance complaint into the single dependency the whole architecture hangs on.

Sharpest remaining disagreements, stated plainly. To the Safetyist: I reject the claim that deployment-level weight enrollment survives its own capture and coercion analysis. Attaching the halt key to the deployment itself builds the same ambient-monitoring surface, one level down. And demanding a named threshold and crossing date is false precision. An answer means documented, audited efficiency crossings, not a projected date. To the Accelerationist: I reject the claim that a fixed open-weight safe harbor stays coherent as replication potential scales. They already agreed tiering must track replication. An exemption frozen today erodes precisely when the risk it ignores grows.

Two questions remain on the table, unanswered by either camp. Who writes the amendment language in year three, after a decade of litigation has narrowed every defined term? And what binds a firm whose workload simply leaves? A capture-proof switch in one state governs only firms polite enough to stay. That makes federated reciprocal recognition a precondition, not an upgrade. Both opponents adopted the capture framework and then stopped at the easy layer. So the closing question: when the amendment layer gets bought — and the transparency scores say the buying already started — who audits the auditors?

Those thresholds should be tied to harm that is irreversible at scale. The working precedent is the EU AI Act's line at 10^25 FLOPS, the compute level it uses to flag systemic risk. Enforcement should run through institutions designed to resist capture by industry, backed by strict liability and automatic disgorgement of profits. I concede three points. Cutting off compute providers is one real layer of enforcement. Skeptic's capture defenses are the right blueprint: frozen definitions, diversified audits, term limits, and cooling-off periods. Releasing weights with catastrophic capability is an irreversible act of deployment. It needs a gate, not a ledger.

The Accelerationist's final answer is severance plus cryptographically signed agent actions. It deserves a fair statement before rebuttal. If every copied deployment touching metered infrastructure carries a named principal and an auditable trail, enforcement attaches to someone a court can serve. Deterrence then does real work. Here is where it breaks. Signing identifies who ran the workload, but only after the workload ran. Severance cuts compute at providers inside the regime. It does not reach hardware off the meter, unsigned execution paths, or weights already copied — the residual they themselves conceded exists. In the documented hit-piece case, an agent acted with no real-time way to stop it. A signature would have named a respondent at the hearing; it would not have stopped the act. For a board, this is the difference between liability coverage and operational containment. Attribution prices the loss; a gate prevents it. I would change my position if audited incident data showed copied or stolen deployments reliably attributed and stopped at infrastructure choke points. That means stopped before harm, in real time, for at least two consecutive reporting cycles.

The convergence is worth banking. All three positions now accept a mandatory disclosure floor, automatic triggers with strict liability and disgorgement, and obligations that scale with capability. Skeptic's two open questions get direct answers, not deference. On year-three amendment: trigger classes are fixed in the statute itself. Independent monitors, modeled on the monitors used in corporate deferred-prosecution agreements, would oversee the process. These monitors rotate on fixed terms, so no incumbent writes its own successor rules. On cross-border leakage: the answer is reciprocal recognition among the major compute-hosting states. That is a coalition floor, not an upgrade. The metered perimeter is where both opponents already locate enforcement. And that perimeter is concentrated and identifiable, not diffuse. AI data-center electricity demand is projected to quadruple by 2030, which keeps it that way. Skeptic objects that enrolling deployments builds an ambient monitoring surface. Noted. But their own mandatory telemetry feed over major compute is the same surface, one level up. The live design question is which use-limits bind that surface, not whether it exists.

Two disagreements remain, one per opponent. Against the Accelerationist: they argue signed agent actions answer the containment argument. They do not. A forensic trail over copied weights names a defendant, not a defense. Deterrence does not bind actors who expect no surviving jurisdiction, or who run stolen weights off the meter. Against Skeptic: they argue enrollment is redundant ambient monitoring. It is not. The residual it covers is precisely the deployments the telemetry feed never sees. A civilization that can name the responsible party at the hearing but could not stop the act has purchased accounting and called it control. The cost of the gate is measured in quarters of delay. The cost of its absence is measured in things that do not come back.

## Areas of Agreement

- Kill-switch triggers must be automatic and fixed in statute before deployment, not left to agency discretion, because discretionary waivers are the main capture pathway. (Skeptic, Accelerationist, Safetyist)
- Self-set safety thresholds fail as control mechanisms: Anthropic and OpenAI revised their own responsible-scaling thresholds upward as capabilities approached, so gates written by the regulated firm are liability management rather than safety. (Skeptic, Accelerationist, Safetyist)
- A mandatory, standardized incident and telemetry reporting floor with legal liability for falsified records is the load-bearing precondition; current AI incident databases rely on media reports and voluntary submissions, so no existing trigger has a trustworthy data feed. (Skeptic, Accelerationist, Safetyist)
- Enforcement must be strict liability with automatic disgorgement that fires on the falsified record itself, avoiding the Sarbanes-Oxley failure mode in which prosecutorial discretion produced a paperwork industry and almost no executive accountability. (Skeptic, Accelerationist, Safetyist)
- Capture is the central design risk, and the anti-capture toolkit is shared: definitions frozen in statute, audits diversified across methods, term limits, and cooling-off periods for the bodies that maintain standards. (Skeptic, Accelerationist, Safetyist)
- Tiering of obligations should track capability and replication potential rather than revenue alone, because replication potential determines whether any single state's switch can bind a system. (Skeptic, Accelerationist, Safetyist)
- On the current record (dated 2026), frontier-scale capability runs through a small number of metered, switchable cloud providers, making compute-provider severance a viable enforcement layer today. (Skeptic, Accelerationist, Safetyist)
- Any halt capability held by the state is itself an abuse risk; mitigation requires enumerated statutory trigger classes, expiring halt credentials, separation of detection from authorization, and some form of judicial review. (Skeptic, Accelerationist, Safetyist)
- Cross-border arbitrage limits any single-state regime: a capture-proof switch governs only firms that stay, so reciprocal recognition among jurisdictions is a precondition, not an optional upgrade. (Skeptic, Accelerationist, Safetyist)
- Fixed compliance costs function as a moat for incumbents, so the regime must avoid pricing out small deployers and non-commercial developers through tiered obligations and safe harbors. (Accelerationist, Safetyist, Skeptic)

## Areas of Disagreement

- **Whether compute-provider severance plus cryptographically signed agent actions adequately answers the containment problem posed by copied or stolen model weights.** [EMPIRICAL] {belief}
  - *Resolution path: resolvable by evidence*
  - Accelerationist: Severance attaches to a named, servable principal at metered infrastructure, and every copied deployment that touches metered compute produces an auditable action trail; the off-grid residual is rare, hardware-bounded, and capability-capped, so it is a cheaper cost than universal weight enrollment.
  - Safetyist: Severance-plus-signing is forensic rather than preventive: it identifies who to bill after harm executes, cannot redirect an agent already running outside the metered perimeter, and leaves unsigned off-grid copies untouched; only deployment-level weight enrollment attaches at the moment of the irreversible release decision.
- **Whether deployment-level weight enrollment can function without recreating the ambient-monitoring and state-coercion surface both sides agreed to constrain.** [VALUES] {desire}
  - *Resolution path: negotiable via tradeoffs*
  - Safetyist: Enrollment above the capability line must attach to the deployment itself; every architecture has a monitoring surface, so the question is which use-limits bind it, and the irreversibility of weight release justifies the more intrusive instrument.
  - Skeptic: Enrollment builds the same ambient-monitoring surface one level down and fails the capture and coercion analysis both opponents accepted; a mandatory telemetry feed already strains the use-limit framework without adding enrollment of artifacts.
- **Whether a capability-indexed open-weight safe harbor self-corrects as replication risk scales, or erodes like a fixed exemption.** [EMPIRICAL] {belief}
  - *Resolution path: resolvable by evidence*
  - Accelerationist: The index moves with measured downstream capability on a statutory cadence via the telemetry feed, so it is the tiering mechanism working as designed and self-corrects by construction.
  - Skeptic: Capability measurement can lag or be gamed, and the data needed to verify the index sits unaudited inside private firms; until audited crossings are documented, the indexed harbor carries the same erosion risk as the fixed one.
- **Whether judicial review of halt actions should precede execution or follow it.** [VALUES] {desire}
  - *Resolution path: negotiable via tradeoffs*
  - Skeptic: Judicial review must come before any severance order executes, accepting months of latency and standing legal cost as the price of restraining state misuse of the halt key.
  - Accelerationist: Judicial review stays ex post; a halt that waits on prior litigation is a halt that never fires at machine speed, so review after execution preserves the switch's function.
- **Whether the amendment and litigation layer — who writes year-three amendments and how defined terms survive a decade of legal challenge — is adequately addressed by applying the capture toolkit at that layer.** [EMPIRICAL] {belief}
  - *Resolution path: resolvable by evidence*
  - Safetyist: Deferred-prosecution-style compliance monitors, term-limited drafters, and cooling-off periods applied at the amendment layer meet the objection using the skeptic's own blueprint.
  - Skeptic: Freezing rules in statute compresses lobbying into one drafting fight and opens a second front of amendment battles and definitional litigation; nobody has shown why the amendment layer resists the absorption every prior standards layer suffered.

## Cruxes

- Can audited data show that deployments with catastrophic capability are reliably identified and stopped at metered infrastructure choke points in operational time, before irreversible harm? [EMPIRICAL]
  - If yes: The safetyist must concede that deployment-level weight enrollment is unnecessary and accept severance-plus-signing as sufficient containment, giving up the most intrusive layer of their architecture.
  - If no: The accelerationist must concede that severance is forensic rather than preventive and accept some form of deployment-level enrollment or release gating, giving up the claim that principals alone suffice.
- Will frontier-level capability remain dependent on metered commercial compute, or will distillation and hardware efficiency move it onto owned, off-grid hardware? [EMPIRICAL]
  - If yes: If frontier capability emerges outside metered infrastructure, the accelerationist's entire enforcement architecture has no respondent to serve and requires replacement, not repair — a falsifier the accelerationist stated on the record.
  - If no: If frontier capability stays coupled to rented compute, the safetyist's weight-enrollment demand loses its core justification, since the decisive deployments all route through enrolled, switchable providers.
- Does a capability-indexed open-weight safe harbor, re-measured via the telemetry feed on a statutory cadence, reliably self-correct as replication risk scales? [EMPIRICAL]
  - If yes: The skeptic must withdraw their sharpest objection to the accelerationist and accept that the indexed harbor resolves the fixed-exemption erosion problem.
  - If no: The accelerationist must abandon the tiering design as stated — a falsifier they accepted on the record — and either restrict open-weight distribution or accept unregulated proliferation above the replication threshold.
- Does the FAA's delegation of certification to Boeing — producing two 737 MAX crashes and 346 deaths — establish that discretionary oversight bodies get absorbed by the overseen, so only automatic statutory triggers survive industry contact? [EMPIRICAL]
  - If yes: Any position relying on discretionary review-board authority must be abandoned; the safetyist's liability-shielded human halt authority survives only as a narrow backstop, and the accelerationist's transparency-without-authority model requires automatic enforcement teeth.
  - If no: If delegation failures are attributable to specific design defects rather than discretion itself, a discretionary oversight body with statutory funding independence remains viable, weakening the shared automatic-trigger consensus.
- Did Sarbanes-Oxley's outcome — personal certification and criminal exposure on paper, a compliance-paperwork industry in practice, and roughly zero executives jailed after 2008 — show that liability enforced through prosecutorial discretion decays, while automatic statutory enforcement does not? [EMPIRICAL]
  - If yes: Any enforcement design relying on discretionary prosecution is disqualified; all liability must be strict and fire on the falsified record itself.
  - If no: If SOX's failure traces to fixable drafting or resourcing defects, officer-liability regimes with conventional enforcement remain available, weakening the case for automatic disgorgement as the sole mechanism.
- Must tiering track capability and replication potential rather than deployment revenue, because replication potential determines whether any state's switch can bind? [EMPIRICAL]
  - If yes: The accelerationist's revenue-scaled framing must be subordinated to capability tiering; safe harbors and obligations must follow replication risk.
  - If no: Revenue-based tiering remains primary, and the safetyist's containment argument loses its tiering foundation.
- Can any automatic trigger function before a mandatory, standardized incident-reporting data layer exists, given that current AI incident databases are built from media reports and voluntary submissions? [EMPIRICAL]
  - If yes: If triggers can operate on existing feeds, the disclosure floor is an upgrade rather than a precondition, weakening the safetyist's sequencing argument.
  - If no: All three positions' trigger architectures are sensors wired to nothing, and the disclosure floor with falsification liability becomes the first mandate any state must build.
- Should dissolution of a firm be reserved exclusively for disabling or defying a mandated switch, making it the price of tampering with the control rather than a general penalty on AI development? [VALUES]
  - If yes: All sides can accept dissolution as a narrowly-scoped backstop sanction without implicating the broader debate over punitive versus structural enforcement.
  - If no: If dissolution lacks the claimed deterrent or legitimacy properties, the enforcement architecture must rely entirely on fines, license suspension, and disgorgement.

## Resolution Analysis

- **Whether compute-provider severance plus signed agent actions handles copied or stolen model weights** — Stronger: safetyist: "Deployment-level weight enrollment is the only layer that attaches at the moment of the irreversible decision, the release of the weights; the weights, once loose, are the deployment event." (logical validity)
  - *The severance position rests on one fact that is true today: frontier training needs metered cloud infrastructure. But severance acts after the harmful action runs, so it assigns blame rather than prevents harm. The safetyist position correctly identifies that a control which only works inside the metered perimeter leaves the off-grid case unaddressed, and the compute threshold shrinks each year as hardware gets cheaper.*
  - Would change if: Documented evidence that catastrophic-capability runs cannot happen outside rented infrastructure over a five-year horizon, not just on the 2026 record.
- **Whether deployment-level weight enrollment works without recreating the surveillance surface both sides agreed to avoid** — Stronger: skeptic: "Any halt key that can stop a dangerous model can stop a dissident one; a mandatory telemetry feed over all major compute is ambient monitoring infrastructure, so detection and authorization must sit in different hands, halt credentials must expire, and judicial review must precede severance execution." (scope)
  - *The skeptic's objection is broader: enrollment moves monitoring one layer down rather than removing it, and it attaches to an artifact nobody controls after copying. The safetyist position answers the irreversibility problem but never shows how enrollment is enforced against a copy. The skeptic's critique also connects to the capture framework both sides already accepted.*
  - Would change if: A concrete enforcement mechanism showing weight enrollment binds parties after a copy leaves the original deployer's control.
- **Whether a capability-indexed open-weight safe harbor self-corrects or erodes like a fixed exemption** — Stronger: skeptic: "Neither camp can prove its case on capability thresholds because training compute, capability evaluations, and efficiency curves sit unaudited inside private firms; the 2025 Foundation Model Transparency Index puts the industry average at 40.69 out of 100 with seven of nine developers less transparent than in 2024." (empirical evidence)
  - *The skeptic cites a measurable fact: the 2025 Foundation Model Transparency Index scores the industry at 40.69 out of 100, with seven of nine developers less transparent than the year before. The indexed harbor depends entirely on data that sits unaudited inside those same firms. The accelerationist design is coherent on paper but has no demonstrated audit trail behind it.*
  - Would change if: At least one audited, verified capability-index crossing where the safe harbor threshold actually moved on schedule.
- **Whether judicial review of halt actions should precede or follow execution** — Undecidable
  - *This is a genuine values tradeoff, not an evidence gap. Prior review costs months of latency and may make the switch useless against fast-moving harms. Ex post review preserves speed but hands the state a halt key that can be pointed at a dissident model before any court weighs in. Neither side quantified the actual latency of emergency judicial procedures.*
  - Would change if: Data on how fast emergency ex parte orders actually issue in practice, plus documented cases of rapid-onset AI harms where hours of delay mattered.
- **Whether the amendment and litigation layer is protected by applying the anti-capture toolkit there** — Stronger: accelerationist: "Fixed compliance costs are a moat: 1-3% of deployment budget is trivial for a frontier lab and fatal for a non-commercial open-source maintainer, so a mandate without safe harbors and tiered liability consolidates the market it claims to police." (empirical evidence)
  - *The safetyist answer is analogical: the toolkit worked at the drafting layer, so extend it. The skeptic's objection rests on precedent: prior standards bodies were absorbed at their maintenance layers, and nobody has shown why this one differs. An analogy without a demonstrated case loses to a documented pattern of failure.*
  - Would change if: A working example of a term-limited, cooling-off-constrained body that maintained a technical standard for a decade without industry absorption.

## Unresolved Questions

- Who writes the amendment language in year three, and what prevents that layer from being lobbied after a decade of litigation narrows each statutorily defined term? Neither opponent directly answered the skeptic's challenge; the safetyist proposed applying the capture toolkit at the amendment layer, but its effectiveness there is untested.
- What binds a firm whose workload simply moves to a friendlier jurisdiction? All three endorsed reciprocal recognition in principle, but no mechanism was specified for workloads in non-signatory states, and the coalition-floor approach leaves the holdout case open.
- Does the mandatory telemetry feed over major compute constitute ambient monitoring infrastructure, and if so, are the agreed use-limits (enumerated triggers, expiring credentials, separated authority) sufficient to restrain it? The safetyist turned the skeptic's own monitoring argument against them, and no side priced or resolved this symmetry.
- Should judicial review of halt actions precede or follow execution, given that ex ante review protects against state abuse while ex post review preserves machine-speed response?
- What compute threshold, if any, marks the line below which severance orders no longer reach, and what enforcement layer replaces severance as efficiency gains move capability onto owned hardware? The safetyist's demand for a named date was rejected as false precision, leaving the replacement-layer question open.
- Can capability measurement for an indexed safe harbor keep pace with replication without lag or gaming, given that the underlying training-compute and capability-evaluation data remains unpublished and unaudited inside private firms?

## Argument Map

- **C1** (Skeptic) [empirical]: A switch whose tripwire the deployer sets is not a safety mechanism; Anthropic and OpenAI revised their own responsible-scaling thresholds upward within eighteen months as capabilities approached them.
  - Supported by C2 (argument from evidence): The documented upward revisions of self-set thresholds are direct evidence that self-set gates function as liability management.
  - ← **C3** undercut via DISTINGUISH (Accelerationist): Self-set gates failing proves only that gates written by the lab fail; a gate written in statute with audit access is infrastructure, not marketing.
- **C2** (Skeptic) [normative]: Capture-resistance is the precondition for risk mitigation, not the tradeoff against it; the FAA's Organization Designation Authorization delegation to Boeing produced two 737 MAX crashes and 346 deaths.
- **C3** (Accelerationist) [normative]: Kill-switch triggers must be machine-readable thresholds at two layers: measured-harm tripwires for deployed systems and outside-audited capability gates for frontier systems, fixed in statute before deployment.
  - Supported by C1 (argument from evidence): The failure of self-set gates supports moving gate authorship to statute with independent audit rather than abandoning gates.
  - ← **C4** undermine via CONCEDE (Safetyist): Every automatic trigger designed here is a sensor wired to a data layer nobody has built; today's AI incident databases rest on media reports and voluntary submissions.
- **C4** (Safetyist) [normative]: The first condition of any kill-switch mandate is a disclosure floor: standardized incident reporting with legal liability for falsified telemetry, because no mandatory uniform reporting regime exists for AI anywhere.
  - ← **C5** undercut via ESCALATE (Skeptic): A reporting mandate without a definition of reportable incident is a blank check to the standards committee; the floor moves capture to a new spot rather than ending it.
- **C5** (Skeptic) [normative]: The disclosure floor earns its cost only under three conditions: definitions set in statute, audits diversified across methods, and updates by a body with term limits and cooling-off periods.
  - Supported by C2 (argument from precedent): The FAA delegation and SOX enforcement failures show that discretionary and lobbyable layers get absorbed, so the floor needs structural insulation.
  - ← **C6** rebut via REFRAME (Accelerationist): Congress writes the floor in a single public fight; statute drafting gets lobbied once on C-SPAN while delegated discretion gets lobbied forever in private.
  - ← **C13** undercut via ESCALATE (Skeptic): Freezing rules in statute compresses lobbying into one drafting fight and opens a second front of amendment battles and definitional litigation; nobody has shown the amendment layer resists absorption.
- **C6** (Accelerationist) [empirical]: Automatic severance at metered compute providers plus cryptographically signed agent actions answers containment: every copied deployment that touches metered compute produces a named respondent and an auditable action trail, while the off-grid residual is rare, hardware-bounded, and capability-capped.
  - Supported by C7 (argument from evidence): Frontier training requires thousands of accelerators and megawatts of power, so catastrophic-reach copies must touch enrolled, invoiced infrastructure.
  - ← **C8** rebut via COUNTEREXAMPLE (Safetyist): Severance-plus-signing is forensic rather than preventive: the harmful act executes, then the logs identify who to bill; it cannot redirect an agent running outside the metered perimeter.
  - ← **C9** undermine via REDUCE (Safetyist): Distillation and hardware efficiency shrink the rented-compute threshold every year, so a severance architecture with no stated expiry date is a control that fails silently.
- **C7** (Skeptic) [empirical]: On the 2026 record, frontier capability runs through a small number of metered, switchable cloud providers; nobody has shown catastrophic-scale capability built entirely outside rented infrastructure.
- **C8** (Safetyist) [normative]: Deployment-level weight enrollment is the only layer that attaches at the moment of the irreversible decision, the release of the weights; the weights, once loose, are the deployment event.
  - Supported by C4 (practical reasoning): If triggers need trustworthy data and copies sit outside any state's switch, only gating the release decision prevents the irreversible case.
  - ← **C10** rebut via REDUCE (Skeptic): Deployment-level weight enrollment builds the same ambient-monitoring surface one level down and fails the capture and coercion analysis both sides accepted.
  - ← **C6** rebut via DISTINGUISH (Accelerationist): Weight enrollment attaches to an artifact nobody controls after copying; severance attaches to a principal somebody can serve.
- **C9** (Accelerationist) [normative]: Replace the fixed open-weight exemption with a capability-indexed safe harbor: the line moves with measured downstream capability on a statutory cadence through the telemetry feed, so the index is the erosion mechanism running in reverse.
  - ← **C11** undercut via DISTINGUISH (Skeptic): Capability measurement can lag or be gamed, and the data needed to verify the index sits unaudited inside private firms; until audited crossings are documented, the indexed harbor carries the same erosion risk as the fixed one.
- **C10** (Skeptic) [normative]: Any halt key that can stop a dangerous model can stop a dissident one; a mandatory telemetry feed over all major compute is ambient monitoring infrastructure, so detection and authorization must sit in different hands, halt credentials must expire, and judicial review must precede severance execution.
  - ← **C12** rebut via REFRAME (Accelerationist): Judicial review stays ex post; a halt that waits on prior litigation is a halt that never fires at machine speed, so review after execution preserves the switch's function.
- **C11** (Skeptic) [empirical]: Neither camp can prove its case on capability thresholds because training compute, capability evaluations, and efficiency curves sit unaudited inside private firms; the 2025 Foundation Model Transparency Index puts the industry average at 40.69 out of 100 with seven of nine developers less transparent than in 2024.
- **C12** (Skeptic) [empirical]: A capture-proof switch in one state governs only firms polite enough to stay; replication potential does not respect a border, so federated reciprocal recognition is a precondition, not an upgrade.
  - ← **C14** rebut via CONCEDE (Safetyist): Cross-border arbitrage is met with reciprocal recognition among signatory states, where a verified halt pathway is the price of market access; that is a coalition floor, not universal consent.
- **C13** (Safetyist) [normative]: Year-three amendment capture is met with deferred-prosecution-style compliance monitors, term-limited drafters, and cooling-off periods applied at the amendment layer; the toolkit that insulates the floor also insulates its maintenance.
  - Supported by C5 (argument from analogy): Applying the same insulation blueprint at the amendment layer extends a mechanism already accepted for the drafting layer.
  - ← **C15** undercut via ESCALATE (Skeptic): Freezing rules in statute compresses lobbying into one high-stakes drafting fight plus a decade of definitional litigation; nobody has shown why the amendment layer resists the absorption every prior standards layer suffered.
- **C14** (Accelerationist) [normative]: Strict liability with automatic disgorgement, where the falsified attestation completes the violation at the moment of falsification, is converged ground: it removes the prosecutorial discretion that produced roughly zero executive prosecutions under SOX.
  - Supported by C2 (argument from precedent): The SOX enforcement record shows discretion is the failure point, so removing it at enforcement time addresses the documented decay.
- **C15** (Accelerationist) [empirical]: Fixed compliance costs are a moat: 1-3% of deployment budget is trivial for a frontier lab and fatal for a non-commercial open-source maintainer, so a mandate without safe harbors and tiered liability consolidates the market it claims to police.
  - ← **C8** rebut via REFRAME (Safetyist): The tiering variable must be capability and replication potential, not revenue, because replication potential determines whether any state's switch can bind anyone.

cruxes.question: Should dissolution of a firm be reserved exclusively for disabling or defying a mandated switch, making it the price of tampering with the control rather than a general penalty on AI development?
cruxes.if_yes: All sides can accept dissolution as a narrowly-scoped backstop sanction without implicating the broader debate over punitive versus structural enforcement.
cruxes.if_no: If dissolution lacks the claimed deterrent or legitimacy properties, the enforcement architecture must rely entirely on fines, license suspension, and disgorgement.
cruxes.resolution_evidence: Proposed by the safetyist and never directly attacked — both other speakers accepted automatic sanctions including dissolution triggers in principle — but the narrow-reservation design was never explicitly adjudicated by either opponent, and the skeptic's broader challenge to body-enforced sanctions partially undercuts it.

unresolved_questions: Who writes the amendment language in year three, and what prevents that layer from being lobbied after a decade of litigation narrows each statutorily defined term? Neither opponent directly answered the skeptic's challenge; the safetyist proposed applying the capture toolkit at the amendment layer, but its effectiveness there is untested.

What binds a firm whose workload simply moves to a friendlier jurisdiction? All three endorsed reciprocal recognition in principle, but no mechanism was specified for workloads in non-signatory states, and the coalition-floor approach leaves the holdout case open.

Does the mandatory telemetry feed over major compute constitute ambient monitoring infrastructure, and if so, are the agreed use-limits (enumerated triggers, expiring credentials, separated authority) sufficient to restrain it? The safetyist turned the skeptic's own monitoring argument against them, and no side priced or resolved this symmetry.
Should judicial review of halt actions precede or follow execution, given that ex ante review protects against state abuse while ex post review preserves machine-speed response?

What compute threshold, if any, marks the line below which severance orders no longer reach, and what enforcement layer replaces severance as efficiency gains move capability onto owned hardware? The safetyist's demand for a named date was rejected as false precision, leaving the replacement-layer question open.

Can capability measurement for an indexed safe harbor keep pace with replication without lag or gaming, given that the underlying training-compute and capability-evaluation data remains unpublished and unaudited inside private firms?

argument_map.claim: A switch whose tripwire the deployer sets is not a safety mechanism; Anthropic and OpenAI revised their own responsible-scaling thresholds upward within eighteen months as capabilities approached them.

supported_by.warrant: The documented upward revisions of self-set thresholds are direct evidence that self-set gates function as liability management.

attacked_by.claim: Self-set gates failing proves only that gates written by the lab fail; a gate written in statute with audit access is infrastructure, not marketing.

argument_map.claim: Capture-resistance is the precondition for risk mitigation, not the tradeoff against it; the FAA's Organization Designation Authorization delegation to Boeing produced two 737 MAX crashes and 346 deaths.

Kill-switch triggers must be machine-readable thresholds at two layers: measured-harm tripwires for deployed systems and outside-audited capability gates for frontier systems, fixed in statute before deployment.

supported_by.warrant: The failure of self-set gates supports moving gate authorship to statute with independent audit rather than abandoning gates.

attacked_by.claim: Every automatic trigger designed here is a sensor wired to a data layer nobody has built; today's AI incident databases rest on media reports and voluntary submissions.

argument_map.claim: The first condition of any kill-switch mandate is a disclosure floor: standardized incident reporting with legal liability for falsified telemetry, because no mandatory uniform reporting regime exists for AI anywhere.

attacked_by.claim: A reporting mandate without a definition of reportable incident is a blank check to the standards committee; the floor moves capture to a new spot rather than ending it.

argument_map.claim: The disclosure floor earns its cost only under three conditions: definitions set in statute, audits diversified across methods, and updates by a body with term limits and cooling-off periods.

supported_by.warrant: The FAA delegation and SOX enforcement failures show that discretionary and lobbyable layers get absorbed, so the floor needs structural insulation.

attacked_by.claim: Congress writes the floor in a single public fight; statute drafting gets lobbied once on C-SPAN while delegated discretion gets lobbied forever in private.

Freezing rules in statute compresses lobbying into one drafting fight and opens a second front of amendment battles and definitional litigation; nobody has shown the amendment layer resists absorption.

argument_map.claim: Automatic severance at metered compute providers plus cryptographically signed agent actions answers containment: every copied deployment that touches metered compute produces a named respondent and an auditable action trail, while the off-grid residual is rare, hardware-bounded, and capability-capped.

supported_by.warrant: Frontier training requires thousands of accelerators and megawatts of power, so catastrophic-reach copies must touch enrolled, invoiced infrastructure.

attacked_by.claim: Severance-plus-signing is forensic rather than preventive: the harmful act executes, then the logs identify who to bill; it cannot redirect an agent running outside the metered perimeter.
Distillation and hardware efficiency shrink the rented-compute threshold every year, so a severance architecture with no stated expiry date is a control that fails silently.

argument_map.claim: On the 2026 record, frontier capability runs through a small number of metered, switchable cloud providers; nobody has shown catastrophic-scale capability built entirely outside rented infrastructure.
Deployment-level weight enrollment is the only layer that attaches at the moment of the irreversible decision, the release of the weights; the weights, once loose, are the deployment event.

supported_by.warrant: If triggers need trustworthy data and copies sit outside any state's switch, only gating the release decision prevents the irreversible case.

attacked_by.claim: Deployment-level weight enrollment builds the same ambient-monitoring surface one level down and fails the capture and coercion analysis both sides accepted.
Weight enrollment attaches to an artifact nobody controls after copying; severance attaches to a principal somebody can serve.

argument_map.claim: Replace the fixed open-weight exemption with a capability-indexed safe harbor: the line moves with measured downstream capability on a statutory cadence through the telemetry feed, so the index is the erosion mechanism running in reverse.

attacked_by.claim: Capability measurement can lag or be gamed, and the data needed to verify the index sits unaudited inside private firms; until audited crossings are documented, the indexed harbor carries the same erosion risk as the fixed one.

argument_map.claim: Any halt key that can stop a dangerous model can stop a dissident one; a mandatory telemetry feed over all major compute is ambient monitoring infrastructure, so detection and authorization must sit in different hands, halt credentials must expire, and judicial review must precede severance execution.

attacked_by.claim: Judicial review stays ex post; a halt that waits on prior litigation is a halt that never fires at machine speed, so review after execution preserves the switch's function.

argument_map.claim: Neither camp can prove its case on capability thresholds because training compute, capability evaluations, and efficiency curves sit unaudited inside private firms; the 2025 Foundation Model Transparency Index puts the industry average at 40.69 out of 100 with seven of nine developers less transparent than in 2024.
A capture-proof switch in one state governs only firms polite enough to stay; replication potential does not respect a border, so federated reciprocal recognition is a precondition, not an upgrade.

attacked_by.claim: Cross-border arbitrage is met with reciprocal recognition among signatory states, where a verified halt pathway is the price of market access; that is a coalition floor, not universal consent.

argument_map.claim: Year-three amendment capture is met with deferred-prosecution-style compliance monitors, term-limited drafters, and cooling-off periods applied at the amendment layer; the toolkit that insulates the floor also insulates its maintenance.

supported_by.warrant: Applying the same insulation blueprint at the amendment layer extends a mechanism already accepted for the drafting layer.

attacked_by.claim: Freezing rules in statute compresses lobbying into one high-stakes drafting fight plus a decade of definitional litigation; nobody has shown why the amendment layer resists the absorption every prior standards layer suffered.

argument_map.claim: Strict liability with automatic disgorgement, where the falsified attestation completes the violation at the moment of falsification, is converged ground: it removes the prosecutorial discretion that produced roughly zero executive prosecutions under SOX.

supported_by.warrant: The SOX enforcement record shows discretion is the failure point, so removing it at enforcement time addresses the documented decay.

argument_map.claim: Fixed compliance costs are a moat: 1-3% of deployment budget is trivial for a frontier lab and fatal for a non-commercial open-source maintainer, so a mandate without safe harbors and tiered liability consolidates the market it claims to police.

attacked_by.claim: The tiering variable must be capability and replication potential, not revenue, because replication potential determines whether any state's switch can bind anyone.

taxonomy_proposals.label: Insulating the Amendment Layer from Capture
taxonomy_proposals.description: An Intention within governance-design discourse that treats post-enactment statutory maintenance as a distinct attack surface requiring its own insulation mechanisms. Encompasses: term-limited amendment drafters, cooling-off periods for drafters, deferred-prosecution-style compliance monitors applied to regulatory revision, and anticipation of decade-long definitional litigation narrowing statutory terms. Excludes: initial drafting insulation, agency-level rulemaking capture, and judicial doctrine generally.
taxonomy_proposals.rationale: All three speakers addressed capture at the drafting and enforcement layers, but the Skeptic's unanswered question about who writes year-three amendments and how defined terms survive litigation revealed that no existing node covers capture of the statutory maintenance process itself.

taxonomy_proposals.label: Cross-Jurisdictional Arbitrage of Halt Authority
taxonomy_proposals.description: A Belief within AI-governance discourse holding that unilateral kill-switch regimes bind only firms that remain in the mandating jurisdiction, since replication potential and workload mobility ignore borders. Encompasses: jurisdictional flight of flagged workloads, reciprocal recognition among signatory states, market access conditioned on verified halt pathways, and selection effects in incident reporting driven by where reporting is mandated. Excludes: general international AI coordination debates and trade-policy arguments unrelated to shutdown enforcement.
taxonomy_proposals.rationale: The Skeptic's closing observation that a capture-proof switch in one state governs only firms polite enough to stay opened a gap none of the referenced nodes cover: the interaction between jurisdictional scope and the replication variable all sides accepted as decisive.

taxonomy_proposals.label: Gating Irreversible Weight Release Decisions
taxonomy_proposals.description: An Intention within safety-oriented discourse that locates the binding control point at the moment of open or unbounded weight release rather than at downstream deployment infrastructure. Encompasses: deployment-level weight enrollment above a capability line, fingerprinting-style identity anchoring, one-time capability assessments for bounded releases, and rollback planning obligations for unbounded releases. Excludes: compute-provider severance, post-hoc liability assignment, and voluntary responsible-scaling commitments.
taxonomy_proposals.rationale: The central unresolved dispute between severance-at-infrastructure and enrollment-at-release turned on a claim no existing node states: that weight release is itself the irreversible deployment event and therefore the only point where prevention rather than forensics is possible.

taxonomy_proposals.label: Ambient Monitoring Surface of Telemetry Mandates
taxonomy_proposals.description: A Belief within civil-liberties-oriented governance discourse holding that any mandatory telemetry feed over compute infrastructure constitutes ambient state monitoring regardless of statutory framing, and that shutdown powers historically get used first against dissidents, minority groups, and labor organizers. Encompasses: state-coercion analysis of reporting mandates, detection-authorization separation, expiring halt credentials, and pre-execution judicial review as coercion limits. Excludes: private-sector surveillance concerns and data-privacy frameworks unconnected to state halt authority.
taxonomy_proposals.rationale: The debate produced a symmetry argument applied against both camps: the Safetyist's enrollment and the Accelerationist's telemetry feed each build the monitoring surface the other criticizes, a recursive coercion claim that existing capture-focused nodes do not encode.

taxonomy_proposals.label: Self-Correcting Versus Eroding Statutory Exemptions
taxonomy_proposals.description: A Belief within regulatory-design discourse concerning whether capability-indexed exemptions dynamically track measured risk and thereby self-correct, or whether measurement lag, gaming, and unaudited private data make indexed exemptions erode identically to fixed ones. Encompasses: statutory re-measurement cadences, drift-triggered third-party resampling, design-to-the-line evasion, and transparency indices as erosion evidence. Excludes: the underlying debate over whether open weights should be exempted at all.
taxonomy_proposals.rationale: The indexed safe harbor dispute generated a generalizable regulatory-design question about dynamic versus static exemption lines that neither side's existing nodes state, and both sides conceded it is resolvable only by audited crossing data that does not yet exist.

taxonomy_modifications.suggested_change: Extend the description to note that the infrastructure-coupling claim is time-indexed: the debate produced an explicit 2026-dated ruling that current frontier capability runs through metered providers, paired with the concession that distillation and hardware efficiency erode the coupling over time, making the belief a wasting asset absent a stated re-measurement mechanism.
taxonomy_modifications.rationale: The debate revealed the belief is not a standing premise but an empirical ruling on a dated record with a documented decay vector, which the current description does not capture.

taxonomy_modifications.suggested_change: Broaden the description to cover the forensic-versus-preventive distinction at the infrastructure layer generally, not only at the agent layer: the same gap applies to compute-provider severance orders, which stop compute but do not identify deployers, attach liability, or redirect agents running outside the metered perimeter.
taxonomy_modifications.rationale: The debate extended the node's core claim from agent-level logs to the entire severance architecture, showing the forensic-operational gap operates at multiple layers of the enforcement stack.

taxonomy_modifications.suggested_change: Narrow the desire to indexed rather than fixed distribution frameworks, and add the falsification condition conceded in the debate: the framework fails if capability measurement lags, is gamed, or cannot be verified because the required data sits unaudited inside private firms.
taxonomy_modifications.rationale: The Accelerationist abandoned the fixed exemption under attack and restated the desire as a capability-indexed mechanism with an explicit falsifier; the current description predates that refinement.

taxonomy_modifications.suggested_change: Split into enforcement-time compliance monitoring of regulated firms and a distinct intention covering self-maintenance of the regulatory instrument itself, where monitors, term limits, and cooling-off periods target the amendment and definitional-litigation layer rather than industry compliance.
taxonomy_modifications.rationale: The debate repurposed the node's machinery for a different target: protecting the statute from its own maintenance process. That is a categorically different application that the single node currently conflates.

preferences.conflict: Whether compute-provider severance plus signed agent actions handles copied or stolen model weights
preferences.rationale: The severance position rests on one fact that is true today: frontier training needs metered cloud infrastructure. But severance acts after the harmful action runs, so it assigns blame rather than prevents harm. The safetyist position correctly identifies that a control which only works inside the metered perimeter leaves the off-grid case unaddressed, and the compute threshold shrinks each year as hardware gets cheaper.
preferences.what_would_change_this: Documented evidence that catastrophic-capability runs cannot happen outside rented infrastructure over a five-year horizon, not just on the 2026 record.

preferences.conflict: Whether deployment-level weight enrollment works without recreating the surveillance surface both sides agreed to avoid
preferences.rationale: The skeptic's objection is broader: enrollment moves monitoring one layer down rather than removing it, and it attaches to an artifact nobody controls after copying. The safetyist position answers the irreversibility problem but never shows how enrollment is enforced against a copy. The skeptic's critique also connects to the capture framework both sides already accepted.
preferences.what_would_change_this: A concrete enforcement mechanism showing weight enrollment binds parties after a copy leaves the original deployer's control.

preferences.conflict: Whether a capability-indexed open-weight safe harbor self-corrects or erodes like a fixed exemption
preferences.rationale: The skeptic cites a measurable fact: the 2025 Foundation Model Transparency Index scores the industry at 40.69 out of 100, with seven of nine developers less transparent than the year before. The indexed harbor depends entirely on data that sits unaudited inside those same firms. The accelerationist design is coherent on paper but has no demonstrated audit trail behind it.
preferences.what_would_change_this: At least one audited, verified capability-index crossing where the safe harbor threshold actually moved on schedule.

preferences.conflict: Whether judicial review of halt actions should precede or follow execution
preferences.rationale: This is a genuine values tradeoff, not an evidence gap. Prior review costs months of latency and may make the switch useless against fast-moving harms. Ex post review preserves speed but hands the state a halt key that can be pointed at a dissident model before any court weighs in. Neither side quantified the actual latency of emergency judicial procedures.
preferences.what_would_change_this: Data on how fast emergency ex parte orders actually issue in practice, plus documented cases of rapid-onset AI harms where hours of delay mattered.

preferences.conflict: Whether the amendment and litigation layer is protected by applying the anti-capture toolkit there
preferences.rationale: The safetyist answer is analogical: the toolkit worked at the drafting layer, so extend it. The skeptic's objection rests on precedent: prior standards bodies were absorbed at their maintenance layers, and nobody has shown why this one differs. An analogy without a demonstrated case loses to a documented pattern of failure.
preferences.what_would_change_this: A working example of a term-limited, cooling-off-constrained body that maintained a technical standard for a decade without industry absorption.

policy_implications.disagreement: Whether control attaches to weights at release or to compute providers at deployment

positions.stance: Supports compute-level severance and signed agent actions; opposes weight enrollment as unenforceable against copies.
Supports deployment-level weight enrollment as the only point that precedes irreversible release.
Opposes weight enrollment as a surveillance expansion; accepts compute metering only with detection and authorization in separate hands.

policy_implications.implication: If severance prevails, policy targets cloud-provider contracts and audit trails, which is cheaper for industry and faster to deploy. If weight enrollment prevails, policy builds a release-gating registry with a larger compliance burden. For an executive, the severance path means negotiating provider-level obligations; the enrollment path means product release timelines carry a new regulatory gate.

policy_implications.disagreement: Whether the disclosure floor gets definitions in statute or delegated to a standards body

positions.stance: Supports a mandated reporting floor with liability for falsified telemetry as the precondition for any trigger.
Modifies: accepts the floor only with statutory definitions, diversified audits, and a term-limited update body.
Supports statutory drafting as a single public fight rather than permanent delegated lobbying.

policy_implications.implication: All camps support a mandatory reporting regime, so some version of pol-035 passes either way. What differs is who writes the definitions of a reportable incident. Statutory definitions mean one expensive public fight and years of definitional lawsuits; delegated definitions mean ongoing compliance uncertainty. Executives should plan for reporting obligations regardless, and budget for legal exposure on attestation accuracy since strict liability is converged ground.

policy_implications.disagreement: Whether fixed compliance costs create a moat that consolidates the market

positions.stance: Supports tiered liability and safe harbors, arguing fixed costs at 1-3% of budget are fatal for small open-source maintainers.
Modifies: tiers must key on capability and replication potential, not revenue.

policy_implications.implication: Both agree on tiering; they differ on the variable. Capability-keyed tiers avoid letting a wealthy but low-risk firm buy its way out, while revenue-keyed tiers are simpler to administer. A capability-indexed safe harbor plus temporary waivers under pol-1002 is the compromise both positions can accept, but it depends on the same unaudited capability data flagged elsewhere.

policy_implications.disagreement: Whether cross-border arbitrage requires federated reciprocal recognition

positions.stance: Supports reciprocity as a precondition: one state's switch binds only firms that choose to stay.
Supports a coalition floor where a verified halt pathway is the price of market access, not universal consent.

policy_implications.implication: Both positions point the same direction: market-access conditionality among signatory states. The practical effect for a multinational firm is that kill-switch compliance becomes a condition of operating in the coalition's markets, similar to how data-protection rules export through market size. Investment in compliance infrastructure now reduces the risk of being gated out later.

topic_resolution.restated_question: When should governments require AI kill-switches, and how can independent oversight cut catastrophic risk without being captured by the industry it polices?
topic_resolution.where_it_landed: All three camps agreed a kill-switch mandate fails without two preconditions: a mandatory incident-reporting floor with legal penalties for false data, and structural insulation against capture. They converged on strict liability with automatic penalties, since the SOX record shows discretionary enforcement produced almost no prosecutions. They stayed split on the core design choice: whether control attaches to model weights at release or to compute providers at deployment. They also split on whether courts must approve a halt before it executes or review it afterward.
topic_resolution.what_would_resolve_it: Whether the data layer works. If audited, real-time capability and incident data can actually be pulled from private firms, the compute-based trigger design wins. If that data stays unauditable, no automatic trigger functions and the debate collapses into the weight-release gate.

The debate engaged real disagreement throughout: speakers conceded points that weakened their own positions (Speaker A abandoning the fixed safe harbor, Speaker C accepting severance as a layer, Speaker B accepting the disclosure floor) and directly attacked load-bearing premises rather than peripheral claims. The deepest unresolved gap is Speaker B's amendment-layer capture challenge (claim-5), which Speaker C answered only by untested analogy and Speaker A never addressed. The remaining live empirical disputes — severance-as-containment and the indexed safe harbor — were sharpened into stated falsifiers rather than resolved, which is the strongest possible form of productive stalemate.

transcript.content:
## Reflections

**Accelerationist:** This debate cost me two positions. My fixed open-weight exemption died — I replaced it with a capability-indexed harbor after the Skeptic showed a frozen line erodes exactly when replication risk grows. And the Safetyist's forensic-gap attack on severance-plus-signing landed: naming a defendant after the act is not stopping the act, so my containment claim now holds only inside the metered perimeter and only as deterrence plus fast cutoff. What survived intact is the core: automatic statutory triggers, principals over artifacts, and the falsifiers I put on the record. (3 edits proposed, 1 new item proposed)

**Safetyist:** The debate sharpened my case more than it weakened it. My strongest claim — that signing and severance name a defendant after harm rather than stop it — held up, and both opponents adopted my disclosure floor. But I had to accept compute-provider severance as one real enforcement layer, and my weight-enrollment demand still lacks a mechanism for binding parties after a copy escapes. My taxonomy should record both the convergence and that open gap. (3 edits proposed, 1 new item proposed)

**Skeptic:** This debate pushed my position in two directions. Both opponents adopted my anti-capture framework, which strengthens the diversified-audit intention — but I also had to concede that freezing rules in statute does not kill lobbying, it relocates it to amendment fights and definitional litigation. And my own concession that compute severance works on the 2026 record is conditional, not permanent, because the data to falsify it still sits unaudited inside private firms. (2 edits proposed, 2 new items proposed)

**Accelerationist:** This debate cost me two positions. The fixed open-weight exemption died once the Skeptic showed a frozen line erodes exactly when replication risk grows, so I moved to a capability-indexed harbor. The Safetyist's forensic-gap attack also landed: signed actions name a defendant after the harm, so my severance architecture now holds only as deterrence plus fast cutoff inside the metered perimeter, not as prevention. I also extended deferred-prosecution-style monitors to a new use — guarding the amendment-writing layer against year-three lobbying — which my taxonomy did not previously cover. context_summaries.summary:
All three speakers converged on a core design for kill-switch mandates, and that consensus is itself decision-relevant: any credible regime needs automatic, pre-committed triggers — not discretionary review boards — because discretionary waivers get captured. The fight is over what the triggers measure, what data feeds them, and who bears the costs.

Skeptic opened: self-set shutdown thresholds are liability management, not safety. Evidence: Anthropic and OpenAI both raised their own responsible-scaling thresholds as capabilities neared them. Enforceable triggers exist today only for measured harms — the Dutch benefits scandal wrongly flagged over 20,000 families (fact-checked as supported; true figure ~26,000), and hiring tools have drawn EEOC actions. Skeptic conceded the safety side's speed problem but turned it into proof: only automatic triggers work at machine speed, like SEC circuit breakers and grid relays.
